power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.094", "p= 0.9845 ", "p= 0.4480 " ), Sentence = c("Although direct thaw exhibited higher mean viability, a paired t-test indicated that this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.094).", "Interaction effect p= 0.9845 Genotype effect p= 0.4480 Respiration state effect p<0.0001", "Interaction effect p= 0.9845 Genotype effect p= 0.4480 Respiration state effect p<0.0001" )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: High-resolution respirometry of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) is widely used to assess mitochondrial function, but reliance on freshly isolated cells limits flexibility and sample batching.
The impact of cryopreservation and post-thaw handling on PBMC mitochondrial respiration remains incompletely defined.

Methods: PBMCs from healthy young adults were analysed under three conditions: freshly isolated, cryopreserved and directly thawed, and cryopreserved followed by overnight recovery in supplemented culture medium.
Mitochondrial respiration was assessed using an Oroboros O2k high-resolution respirometer following plasma membrane permeabilisation and a substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration protocol.
Respiration parameters included leak, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), maximal uncoupled respiration, and non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
Results: Directly thawed PBMCs exhibited reduced ATP-coupled and maximal respiratory flux compared with fresh cells, indicating acute cryopreservation-induced mitochondrial suppression.
In contrast, PBMCs undergoing overnight recovery showed substantial restoration of mitochondrial function, with OXPHOS and uncoupled respiration closely approximating those of fresh cells.
Cell viability was comparable across conditions.
Cryopreserved PBMCs can be reliably used for mitochondrial respirometry when an overnight recovery step is included.
This approach enables sample storage, batching, and broader application in large-scale and retrospective human studies.
Metabolic processes generate the metabolites required for cell survival and proliferation, with mitochondria playing a central role in coordinating these pathways.
Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which occurs via the electron transport chain (ETC) located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, is essential for ATP production in most mammalian cells [1].
text.formatted: Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which occurs via the electron transport chain (ETC) located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, is essential for ATP production in most mammalian cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Through this process, energy substrates derived from glucose, amino acids, and lipids are converted into ATP to sustain cellular function.
Because oxygen consumption is tightly coupled to ATP production, changes in mitochondrial respiration can directly influence cellular and systemic metabolic function [2].
text.formatted: Because oxygen consumption is tightly coupled to ATP production, changes in mitochondrial respiration can directly influence cellular and systemic metabolic function <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Mitochondrial dysfunction occurs when mitochondria fail to perform optimally and is often associated with mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or nuclear DNA (nucDNA) encoding mitochondrial components [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: Mitochondrial dysfunction occurs when mitochondria fail to perform optimally and is often associated with mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or nuclear DNA (nucDNA) encoding mitochondrial components <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: It can also be characterised by increased production of reactive oxygen species, reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and impaired protein assembly [6].
text.formatted: It can also be characterised by increased production of reactive oxygen species, reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and impaired protein assembly <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, growing evidence links mitochondrial dysfunction to a range of metabolic and systemic diseases [7] [8] [9] [10].
text.formatted: Importantly, growing evidence links mitochondrial dysfunction to a range of metabolic and systemic diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Accurate assessment of mitochondrial function is therefore critical for understanding both physiological and pathological processes.
Over time, various optimised methods have been developed to measure mitochondrial function at both the tissue and cellular levels [11, 12].
text.formatted: Over time, various optimised methods have been developed to measure mitochondrial function at both the tissue and cellular levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: However, many of these approaches require freshly isolated samples to ensure reliable measurements.

Freeze-thaw processes can disrupt mitochondrial membranes, promote the loss of cytochrome c from the intermembrane space, and uncouple oxygen consumption from ATP synthesis, thereby impairing ETC activity [13].
text.formatted: Freeze-thaw processes can disrupt mitochondrial membranes, promote the loss of cytochrome c from the intermembrane space, and uncouple oxygen consumption from ATP synthesis, thereby impairing ETC activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: These limitations present a significant challenge for both basic and translational research, as they restrict the ability to batch samples, reduce costs, and analyse stored specimens.

Recent work by Acín-Pérez et al. (2020) [14] introduced a novel approach to measure mitochondrial respiration in frozen biological samples, demonstrating that respiratory function can be partially preserved under specific experimental conditions.
text.formatted: Recent work by Acín-Pérez et al. (2020) <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> introduced a novel approach to measure mitochondrial respiration in frozen biological samples, demonstrating that respiratory function can be partially preserved under specific experimental conditions.

text.text: Using murine tissues and human cell lines, the study showed that, when combined with plasma membrane permeabilisation and appropriate substrate-inhibitor conditions, oxygen consumption rates could be maintained across fresh and frozen specimens.
However, these findings were obtained using Seahorse XF96 microplate-based assays, and their applicability to high-resolution respirometry in primary human cells remains unclear.

Therefore, the aim of this study was to PREPRINT determine whether mitochondrial function measured in cryopreserved human PBMCs reflects that of freshly isolated PBMCs, and to assess whether an overnight recovery period following thawing can restore mitochondrial respiration.
Establishing such a workflow would enable more flexible experimental designs, including sample batching, multi-site studies, and retrospective analyses using biobanked specimens
Six healthy young participants (n = 3 male, n = 3 female) were recruited for this study.
Participants were free from cardiovascular and metabolic disease and from any injuries that would preclude blood donation.
Inclusion criteria required no blood donation within the previous 24 h and absence of medications or substances that could influence physiological responses.
Written informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
The study was approved by the Auckland Human Participants Ethics Committee (reference 010558).
Participants arrived at the laboratory at 0700-0800 after an overnight fast and had abstained from physical activity for at least 48 h before the visit.
Approximately 45-50 ml of resting venous blood was collected into K2-EDTA Vacutainer tubes and used to isolate PBMCs.

PBMCs were isolated from whole blood by 50 mL SepMate™ tubes (STEMCELL Technologies), which were loaded with 15mL density gradient centrifugation (Ficoll-Paque Plus; GE Healthcare Life Sciences) and centrifuged for 1min to enable the Ficoll to sit below the membrane. 35 mL of diluted blood was then carefully layered onto the membrane, and samples were centrifuged at 1200 x g for 10 minutes, with the brake on at room temperature (RT).
Following centrifugation, mononuclear cells were harvested from the sample/medium interface using a Pasteur pipette.
Cells were subsequently washed twice in room temperature RPMI-1640-medium (non-supplemented) to remove residual Ficoll.
In all cases, isolation of PBMCs commenced within 1 h of the collection of a whole-blood sample.
Isolated cells were manually counted and assessed as > 99% viable using trypan blue.
text.formatted: Isolated cells were manually counted and assessed as > 99% viable using trypan blue.

text.text: Cells for mitochondrial respiration analysis (12-16 million cells total) were pelleted and resuspended in respiration media (MiR05), and PBMC mitochondrial respiration was evaluated 2-3 h after initial blood draw.
The remaining PBMCs were snap-frozen and stored at -80°C overnight before being transferred to long-term storage in liquid nitrogen.

PREPRINT PBMC cryopreservation involved first preparing a 2× cryopreservation medium (DMSO + FBS), stored at -20 °C and thawed at 37 °C before use, followed by careful removal of the supernatant to leave the cell pellet intact, then resuspension in culture medium (fully supplemented RPMI-1640-medium (10% FBS, 1% PS, 1% GlutaMAX).

The cryopreservation medium, pre-cooled to 4 °C, was then added dropwise at a 1:1 volume ratio to the cell suspension to reach a final 10% DMSO concentration, ensuring gentle mixing and reduced osmotic shock.
Cells were aliquoted at 1 mL per cryovial (typically across multiple tubes per donor), with mixing steps such as vortexing to maintain consistency.

The cryovials were immediately placed into an isopropanol-filled controlled-rate freezing container (Mr Frosty) and stored at -80 °C overnight before transfer to liquid nitrogen for long-term storage (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The cryovials were immediately placed into an isopropanol-filled controlled-rate freezing container (Mr Frosty) and stored at -80 °C overnight before transfer to liquid nitrogen for long-term storage (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Finally, sample quality was evaluated by post-thaw viability testing compared with fresh cells.
Cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂.

For overnight recovery experiments, cryopreserved PBMCs were thawed, washed in RPMI 1640 (wash media; Table 1), and resuspended in fully supplemented RPMI (RF10; Table 1: RPMI 1640 with 10% FBS, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX™).
text.formatted: For overnight recovery experiments, cryopreserved PBMCs were thawed, washed in RPMI 1640 (wash media; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), and resuspended in fully supplemented RPMI (RF10; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>: RPMI 1640 with 10% FBS, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX™).

text.text: Cells were plated in ultra-low attachment 6-well plates (Corning Costar®) and cultured overnight prior to analysis (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Cells were plated in ultra-low attachment 6-well plates (Corning Costar®) and cultured overnight prior to analysis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: PBMCs that were thawed and allowed to recover overnight in fully supplemented RPMI prior to analysis.
For both panels, mitochondrial respiration was measured using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2k) following plasma membrane permeabilisation with digitonin.

A standardized substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration protocol was used to quantify leak respiration, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), maximal uncoupled respiration, and non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
PBMC suspensions for oxygraph analysis, whether fresh or cryopreserved, were processed using identical steps to ensure consistency.
Cells were diluted dropwise with prewarmed wash media (RPMI 1640, Table 1) and gently mixed to obtain a homogeneous suspension, with cryopreserved samples fully thawed prior to processing (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Cells were diluted dropwise with prewarmed wash media (RPMI 1640, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>) and gently mixed to obtain a homogeneous suspension, with cryopreserved samples fully thawed prior to processing (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: For overnight-cultured PBMCs, cells were harvested into 15 mL tubes containing wash media.
All samples were centrifuged at 300 × g for 5-7 min at room temperature, and the supernatant PREPRINT was carefully removed without disturbing the pellet.
Cells were washed twice and resuspended in MiR05 buffer at an appropriate volume for cell counting and downstream analysis (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Cells were washed twice and resuspended in MiR05 buffer at an appropriate volume for cell counting and downstream analysis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: Mitochondrial respiration was measured using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2k; Oroboros Instruments, Innsbruck, Austria) with a substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration (SUIT) protocol (Figure 3) [15] [16] [17].
text.formatted: Mitochondrial respiration was measured using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2k; Oroboros Instruments, Innsbruck, Austria) with a substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration (SUIT) protocol (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Measurements were performed in duplicate using 6-8 × 10⁶ cells per chamber.
PBMCs were permeabilised with digitonin (final concentration: 3-4 μM) added to the oxygraph chamber before the respiration titration protocol commenced.
Mitochondrial respiration was measured in a range of states representing nonphosphorylating (leak), phosphorylating (oxphos), and uncoupled respiration.
Complex I (CI) leak respiration was PREPRINT measured with the addition of malate (2 mM) and pyruvate (5 mM), following which ADP (2.5 mM) was added to measure CI oxphos.
Succinate was then added to measure oxphos supported by complex I and II substrates (CI and II oxphos).
Oligomycin was then added to inhibit ATP synthase to measure CI and CII leak respiration.
Stepwise titrations of 0.5 M CCCP were then added to uncouple respiration from oxidative phosphorylation before respiration was inhibited at complex III (CIII) with antimycin A.

All respiration rates were corrected for non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption using the oxygen consumption rate determined following inhibition of CIII, and the CIV respiration rate was corrected for auto-oxidation in each assay.
All mitochondrial respiration rates were recorded and quantified using Datlab 6.1 software (Oroboros Instruments).
Data are expressed as respiration rate per million cells for PBMCs.
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).
Data are presented as mean ± SEM.
Comparisons between fresh and frozen PBMC conditions were performed using paired t-tests.
Statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05.

text.text: PBMCs collected from six healthy volunteers were used to determine optimal conditions for downstream assays.
Participants had a mean age of 34.0 ± 4.22 years and a mean body mass index (BMI) of 29.28 ± 7.93 kg/m².
Each volunteer donated 50-60 mL of whole blood, from which PBMCs were isolated and used for this study.

Table 2: Participant characteristics Participant characteristics Mean ± S.E.M Age (years) 34.0 ± 4.22 Height (cm) 180.6 ± 4.33 Weight (kg) 105.1 ±16.48 Body mass index (m/kg 2 ) 29.3 ± 7.93 S.E.M. standard error of the mean.

Following revival of PBMCs from cryogenic storage (2 weeks to 1 month), cell viability was compared between two recovery approaches: direct thawing and overnight culture, to determine the most reliable method for downstream assays.
Frozen vials were rapidly thawed, transferred into 15 mL of pre-warmed RPMI 1640, and centrifuged at 200 × g for 2 minutes at room temperature to remove DMSO.
Cells were washed twice with fresh RPMI and resuspended in 5 mL of complete culture media (RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX™).
PBMCs were then plated at a density of 2 × 10⁶ cells per well in 24-well plates and either assessed immediately or after an overnight recovery period.

Viability analysis revealed no significant difference between directly thawed and overnight-cultured cells (Table 3; Figure 4), indicating that both approaches provide comparable outcomes and supporting the robustness of the culture workflow for cryopreserved PBMCs.
text.formatted: Viability analysis revealed no significant difference between directly thawed and overnight-cultured cells (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>), indicating that both approaches provide comparable outcomes and supporting the robustness of the culture workflow for cryopreserved PBMCs.

text.text: Cryopreservation and thawing can induce membrane and metabolic stress in PBMCs, transiently altering oxidative phosphorylation.

Following our comparison of PBMC viability between direct-thaw and overnight-culture conditions (Figure 4), we then compared freshly isolated PBMCs with directly thawed and thawed-then-recovered cells to determine whether an overnight recovery step could restore mitochondrial respiration toward fresh profiles.
text.formatted: Following our comparison of PBMC viability between direct-thaw and overnight-culture conditions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>), we then compared freshly isolated PBMCs with directly thawed and thawed-then-recovered cells to determine whether an overnight recovery step could restore mitochondrial respiration toward fresh profiles.

text.text: We hypothesised that culturing cells overnight in fully supplemented RPMI would help minimise these stress effects, normalise nutrient uptake, and provide a more physiologically relevant condition for comparison with freshly isolated PBMCs.

This experimental design enabled us to determine whether cryopreservation affects the mitochondrial phenotype, informing whether PBMCs can be frozen and subsequently used for mitochondrial function measurements.

In addition, it allowed us to assess changes in mitochondrial respiration associated with freezing and recovery, independent of cell viability, which remained comparable across all conditions (Figure 5).

text.text: In this study, we established a workflow incorporating PBMC isolation, cryopreservation, postthaw recovery, and high-resolution respirometry to evaluate the feasibility of measuring mitochondrial respiration in frozen human PBMCs.
Our findings demonstrate that cryopreserved PBMCs can be reliably used for high-resolution respirometry when an overnight recovery period is included following thawing.

This is particularly relevant given that cryopreservation is known to induce transient mitochondrial stress, reduce oxidative phosphorylation efficiency, and alter respiratory fluxes across a range of primary cell types [13, 18, 19].
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant given that cryopreservation is known to induce transient mitochondrial stress, reduce oxidative phosphorylation efficiency, and alter respiratory fluxes across a range of primary cell types <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: High-resolution respirometry is widely used to assess mitochondrial function in tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, brain, and heart.
However, validated approaches for frozen PBMCs remain limited, with relatively few studies directly addressing methodological constraints in these cells [20].
text.formatted: However, validated approaches for frozen PBMCs remain limited, with relatively few studies directly addressing methodological constraints in these cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: This limitation has restricted the use of PBMCs in large-scale or multi-centre human studies, where immediate processing of fresh samples is often impractical.
A recognised challenge in PBMC-based respirometry is cellular heterogeneity and platelet contamination, both of which can influence oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurements.
Platelets, which have a high mitochondrial density, can co-purify with PBMCs and potentially lead to overestimation of mitochondrial respiration if not adequately controlled [11].
text.formatted: Platelets, which have a high mitochondrial density, can co-purify with PBMCs and potentially lead to overestimation of mitochondrial respiration if not adequately controlled <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Despite these challenges, previous studies have reported that cryopreserved PBMCs retain approximately 90-95% of the maximal respiratory capacity observed in freshly isolated cells cells [20].
text.formatted: Despite these challenges, previous studies have reported that cryopreserved PBMCs retain approximately 90-95% of the maximal respiratory capacity observed in freshly isolated cells cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with these observations, our data indicate that mitochondrial respiratory capacity is largely preserved following cryopreservation when an appropriate recovery period is applied [21].
text.formatted: Consistent with these observations, our data indicate that mitochondrial respiratory capacity is largely preserved following cryopreservation when an appropriate recovery period is applied <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Direct analysis of PBMCs immediately after thawing revealed attenuated oxidative phosphorylation and reduced maximal respiratory capacity, consistent with acute cryopreservation-associated mitochondrial suppression.
Importantly, these changes were not accompanied by reduced cell viability, suggesting that cryopreservation primarily induces functional, rather than cytotoxic, alterations.

Following overnight recovery in fully supplemented culture conditions, mitochondrial respiratory profiles closely approximated those of freshly isolated PBMCs, supporting the inclusion of a recovery step as a critical component of the experimental workflow.
This study has several limitations.
The sample size was modest (n = 6), and all participants were healthy young adults, which may limit the generalisability of these findings to older individuals or clinical populations.
In addition, PBMC heterogeneity was not further characterised, and differences in cell subset composition may contribute to variability in mitochondrial measurements.
Future studies should address these factors and assess the applicability of this workflow across diverse cohorts and disease states.
Overall, these findings validate a practical and reproducible framework for assessing mitochondrial respiration in cryopreserved PBMCs using high-resolution respirometry.

Incorporation of an overnight recovery period overcomes a key limitation associated with reliance on freshly isolated cells, enabling sample batching, multi-site study designs, and retrospective analysis of biobanked material.
This approach broadens the applicability of PBMC-based mitochondrial phenotyping in human research.
